paras: The killing of an unidentified Black man at the Blanco River took place on July 29, 1881, when a deputy sheriff of Hays County, Texas, shot him dead near the railroad bridge over the river. The deputy was said to have fired because the man resisted arrest, and neither man's name reached the press. The killing is known from a single brief Austin dispatch whose headline called the dead man a cattle thief, a charge the dispatch itself did not make.

According to a special telegram from Austin dated July 30, "a report reached here to-day" that a deputy sheriff of "Hayes county" had, the day before, "shot and killed a negro for resisting arrest." The dispatch placed the killing near the railroad bridge on the Blanco River and added that "the names of the parties are not known." It did not say what the man was to be arrested for, how he resisted, or whether anyone else was present.
No report of an inquest, an identification of either man, or any action against the deputy appears in the coverage found.

The Dallas Daily Herald printed the item on July 31 as one paragraph in a "State Specials" column of Austin news, between a railroad charter amendment and an accidental death at a wood camp. Its deck headline summarized the item as "Negro Cattle-Thief Shot and Killed in Hays County," and the dispatch repeated the officer's justification of resisting arrest without attribution or question. No other newspaper account was found, and the Black-press collection does not reach back to 1881.

The cattle-stealing charge appears only in the headline. The same column reported that Constable Kroose had arrested one George Thomas in Austin, "accused of cattle stealing in Hayes county," but it did not give his race or connect him to the shooting, so the headline may have joined two separate items.
